title: Your Managers Aren't Routers
author: Brian Elliott
summary: Brian Elliott previews findings from the Charter AI Pulse, a survey of 5,002 US desk workers who use AI on the job plus more than 90 interviews, and draws leadership lessons from it. He reports that 42.7% of AI users say AI is making work and life better but only 10.5% are thriving, and that most benefits come from people teaching themselves because 21.4% received no training at all. Executives are twice as likely as workers to trust AI output over their own judgment, which he reads as a sign that leaders are handing off the most thinking. Against the argument that AI can replace the information-routing middle manager, the data show eleven of the top 14 factors tied to benefiting from AI are controlled by managers, who also hide their own AI use out of fear of looking incompetent. He closes with four actions: go undercover, make managers the investment, train hands-on at the team level, and give people agency over how AI fits their jobs.
points: Elliott's central claim is that managers are the single biggest lever for AI benefit, because eleven of the top 14 factors that predict benefit are things managers control.

Executives are twice as likely as workers to trust AI output over their own judgment (32.8% vs. 16.3%), which he links to AI being good at producing the summaries and clean drafts executives are used to consuming.
A demonstration gap exists: 54.7% of managers say they use AI visibly, but only 30.4% of workers see it, and managers are 1.6 times as likely as workers to conceal their use.
Agency beats advanced technique: whether people have a say in how AI fits their job is the strongest predictor of benefit, yet only 37% of workers have it.
Treating AI purely as an efficiency play invites resistance, while the companies pulling ahead are designing work around motivation and capability and are growing headcount.
quotes: The finding that drew the most interest: executives are twice as likely as workers to trust AI output over their own judgment (32.8% vs. 16.3%), and more than twice as likely to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague (33.1% vs. 15.8%).
So if your CEO thinks AI should have doubled everyone’s output by now, ask them when they last did the work themselves? Not review it, do it, by the rules of the organization.

Most of the people who are benefiting from using AI got there on their own. 21.4% of AI users say their organization has provided no training or support at all, and fewer than 40% get the hands-on training they rate as most useful.

Eleven of the top 14 factors tied to employees benefiting from AI come down to factors their managers control, actions they take, cultures they set. Managers are the single biggest lever you have, and the Charter AI Pulse shows how badly we’ve underinvested in them.
Managers are the secret AI users. They’re 1.6 times as likely as workers to hide their own AI use (43.7% vs. 27.1%), and nearly half of them say it’s out of fear of looking incompetent.
Managers need time, permission, real use cases, and a job description that makes building their team’s capability part of the work, and they need it now.
The strongest factor is agency: whether people have a say in how AI fits into their job is the strongest factor when it comes to whether or not people are seeing the benefits of using AI at work.
If you treat AI purely as an efficiency play, a way to get the same work from fewer people, expect massive resistance.
